recentItems.title: 25 Years on: How 9/11 changed the world | The Bottom Line
recentItems.description:
In “All the President’s Wars,” Peter Bergen argues that every US president since the Al-Qaeda attacks of 2001 has “accrued more power” for the presidency.
 
Bush invaded Iraq, which had nothing to do with fighting Al-Qaeda. Obama became the “drone president,” launching attacks in countries not at war with the US. With the rise of the national security state, Obama could get approval for $120 billion for military spending, but not $2 billion for early childhood education.
 
Bergen tells host Steve Clemons that it’s still an open question whether 9/11 marked “the beginning of the end of American global dominance.”

recentItems.title: Houthis pledge to continue attacks on ‘Saudi military concentrations until aggression ceases’
recentItems.description:
Yemen's Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree has announced a large-scale military operation targeting military infrastructure at King Khalid military base in Khamis Mushait, Saudi Arabia, using dozens of ballistic missiles and drones. He said the operation was in retaliation for more than 300 Saudi airstrikes over the past five days, which used F-15 and Typhoon warplanes taking off from Khamis Mushait and Al-Taif military bases. Saree claimed the missiles hit targets with absolute precision, causing grave losses and damage at the base. He vowed the Houthis will continue operations in the depth of Saudi territory as long as what he called "unjust aggression" continues, warning that any further aggression will be met with larger operations: "We will continue escalation to escalation and siege to siege." The statement was issued on 14 September 2026. The Houthis now control over 90% of Yemen's Red Sea coastline, including the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital route for international shipping, and have warned that all Saudi vessels will be targeted.

recentItems.title: Yemen gov’t forces advance in Taiz as Houthis claim attack on Saudi Arabia
recentItems.description:
Yemen's Ansar Allah Houthis say they have fired dozens of drones and ballistic missiles at military targets in Saudi Arabia, including Khamis Mushait and the King Khalid Air Base. They say the attacks are in retaliation for more than 300 Saudi air strikes inside Yemen over the past five days. Riyadh is supporting the internationally recognised government, which is battling Houthi territorial gains. Video released by the Saudi-backed Yemeni army appears to show the Air Force targeting Houthi positions and vehicles in Taiz. The Houthis control most of the north and west, including the capital Sanaa, while the government and allied forces control much of the south and east. Fighting is concentrated in Taiz, Mocha and Marib. The Houthis have vowed to continue their attacks until Saudi Arabia ceases its aerial bombardment. Since the conflict escalated, Saudi Arabia and its allies have carried out more than 250,000 air strikes, yet the Houthis have continued expanding southwards to Bab al-Mandab and Mocha by mastering stealth warfare. On the humanitarian front, the International Organization for Migration says nearly 100,000 civilians have been displaced from western Taiz, al-Bayda, Marib and al-Jawf. The latest fighting could lead to another humanitarian catastrophe, with Yemen only recently emerging from what was described as the world's worst humanitarian crisis, including widespread malnutrition and hospitals struggling to function. 

Al Jazeera's Yousef Mawry reports from Sanaa.

recentItems.title: Iran’s FM spokesperson says Saudi Arabia requested postponement of Oman talks with Gulf states
recentItems.description:
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei has held a wide-ranging media briefing in Tehran. He accused the US of perpetrating war crimes in the city of Lamerd on the first day of US-Israel attacks on Iran, saying cluster missiles were used and that 21 civilians, including children and visitors from Afghanistan, were killed, with schools, public facilities and a blood bank affected. 
He also said a commercial vessel was targeted near Hengam Island, killing one Iranian, and injuring two others, including Pakistani citizens. 
Baghaei confirmed that Saudi Arabia requested the postponement of the planned Oman meeting between Iran and GCC states and said the Iran-Oman agreement on maritime routes is "almost sealed", with a joint meeting intended to present it to all regional states. 
On the Houthi advances in Yemen, he said Iran does not interfere in Yemeni affairs and is not involved in what is unfolding there, describing Ansar Allah Houthis as an independent body making its own decisions. 
He rejected reports of an Iranian role in an attack on Saudi Arabia from Iraq as "false" and "baseless" US propaganda aimed at dividing regional countries. 
On reports about nuclear facilities at Pickaxe Mountain, he called them part of a "media and psychological warfare" campaign and "baseless, groundless reports". 
He also said Iran can never be isolated, pointing to BRICS support and even US allies such as Canada challenging what he described as Washington's unipolar order.

recentItems.title: DR Congo families live among ruins three days after deadly Bukavu fire
recentItems.description:
Families in Bukavu are living amid the debris of a fire that killed at least 29 people, most of them children, as authorities bar reconstruction until urban planning teams assess the damage. Survivors like Bienfait Lujanga and Yvette Mwabirinda, both parents of large families, have been left homeless, relying on temporary shelter. Schools deemed unsafe have also been shut. A collective burial for the victims, including nine-year-old Cynthia Luaboshi, took place on Monday as the community mourns and awaits permission to rebuild.

Al Jazeera’s Alain Uaykani reports from Bukavu, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

recentItems.title: Gulf states must engage directly with Iran as US security role wanes, analyst says
recentItems.description:
Planned talks in Oman between Iran and GCC states have been postponed, officially to create conditions for constructive dialogue. Meanwhile, the Houthis have been cementing their control of the Bab al-Mandab area. Sultan Barakat, professor of public policy at Hamad bin Khalifa University, told Al Jazeera that the Oman meeting was the result of a mediated process, not an Iranian invitation, with Gulf states trying to get Iran around the table for regional arrangements, knowing they cannot rely on the United States and do not want direct confrontation with Iran. He said the war started as a short operation but is now entering its seventh month, with Gulf states paying the highest price. Barakat explained that Bahrain is opposed to the talks in principle and will not sit with Iran until diplomatic relations are restored, while Saudi Arabia is worried about being presented with a fait accompli — an Oman-Iran plan discussed for months — and feels Iran is playing a double game by talking while using forces to stir trouble. Other countries, particularly Qatar, Iraq and Kuwait, are in a difficult position as they struggle to restore export levels and lose markets, with the US not helping by subsidising the market. Barakat noted there is no supply crisis like those seen in the 1970s, but supplies are more expensive. On the recent strike on the Saudi East-West pipeline, he said it would be a mistake to assume the Houthis only act on Iran's orders, arguing that Arab states should talk directly to them, recognise their grievances and seek agreements. He added that Saudi Arabia is capable of neutralising regional forces if it has the will, and that the realisation that outside powers cannot protect them should drive Gulf states towards direct talks with Iran.
